1890-91. 


ADVANTAGES FOR YOUNG MEN 
ie ae ab NEW BUILDING 


DOMINION SQUARE. 
—<—<—_ ey 


This will be one of the most attractive resorts in the City. 


A profitable use of the leisure time of Young Men. 


The Physieal Department will include a well-equipped 
. Gymnasium, with Physical Instruction and Medical Examina- 
tion; Swimming, Shower, Needle and Sponge Baths, and 
Bowling Alleys ; 700 Lockers, fitted with Combination Locks. 


The Edueational Department will include a beautifully- 
lighted and well-furnished Reading Room and _ Library, 
Evening Classes, Lectures and Entertainments. 


The Religious Department, with its Young Men’s Meetings, 


Courses of Bible Training Classes for Workers, Evangelistic 


Bible Classes, and other plans of personal religious work 
amongst young men. 


The Junior Department, including Boys from 12 to 16 years 
of age, will have separate Reading Room, Library, Parlors and 
Meeting Room, and special hours for use of the Gymnasium. 
This will be distinct from the general work for Young Men. 


In order to place this Building and its advantages within the reach 
of the Commercial, Mechanical and Student Young Men of the city, 
the Directors have decided to place the Tickets of Membership at 
the following rates :—

AOTH AI NU ATOR RB PORT. 


BOARD OF DIRECTORS. 


In reviewing the record of the Young Men’s Christian Association of this City for 
the past year, it must be remembered that the whole work has been in a state of 
transition, and as a consequence new lines of work have not been undertaken. 

The Directors have held 17 meetings and have had under discussion many perplex- 
ing and difficult questions, The attendance at Directors’ Meetings has been larger 
than usual and the heavy demand upon their time and personal attention has been 
most freely given. 

THE VICTORIA SQUARE BUILDING. 


A satisfactory sale of the present building and property was found to be impossi- 
ble, on account of the condition of the western gable wall. In February last the City 
Building Inspector condemned it and demanded its demolition and re-construction. 
An agreement was finally arrived at between the Association and Mr. Gravel, the 
owner of the adjoining building and the joint owner of the wall, by which the 
Association rebuilds the wall and Mr. Gravel withdraws all claims for damages. 
The work is now being done under the supervision of Mr. A. C. Hutchison as 
architect. The Building has been leased for a term of three years to suitable tenants. 
At the end of this time and when placed in thorough repair, on account of its com- 
manding position it will doubtless be a more valuable asset for the Association. 


DOMINION SQUARE BUILDING. 


The time of the Officers had to be given almost wholly to the affairs of the new 
Building. The Directors hope this will be opened to the members in September 
and are making generous plans for the complete equipment and working of the 
following departments :— 

THE JUNIOR DEPARTMENT, 


including a separate Realing Koom, Library and Social Room, will be under the 
supervisidn of Mr, D. W. Corbett, who returns from the Springfield Training School as 
Assistant Secretary. 

THE PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT, 


including the Gymnasium, with instruction in graded classes and Physical examina- 
tion, Swimming, Shower and Sponge Baths, Bowling Alleys and 700 lockers fitted 
with combination locks, all to be under the supervision of Mr. W.H. Ball, jr., of 
Yonkers, N.Y. This gentleman is a competent Physical Instructor and is as much 
at home in leading a Young Men’s Meeting or Bible Class as he is in directing a 
class on the floor of the Gymnasium. 


THE EDUCATIONAL DEPARTMENT, 


with Evening Classes in Commercial and Mechanical branches and languages, 
under competent teachers; in fact the aim of the Association will be to make this 
Department a practical ‘‘Aventng College for day workers.” 


THE SOCIAL DEPARTMENT, 


with suitably furnished Parlors and Recreation Rooms, which will offer to the 
members and to the young strangers an opportunity to be helped from falling into 
bad social surroundings. While the Association can never be the substitute for the 
home, it may be so pervaded by that spirit which makes home the happiest 
spot on earth, that the young men in boarding houses will find in it very much that 
he is deprived of elsewhere in his City life. 

Above all these lines of work 


THE RELIGIOUS WORK DEPARTMENT 


will have its special schedules of Young Men’s Meetings, Bible and Training 
Classes, and Public Addresses on pertinent religious themes. This will be under care- 
ful supervision and interwoven throughout the whole work, for if the young man was 
cared for in the lines indicated above and his spiritual life neglected, the Association 
would be recreant to its highest purpose. 

The Committees, to be named at the first meeting of the Directors, will be called 
upon to give their best attention and efforts to the preparation of complete details, so 
that no time may be lost when the Building is opened. 


FINANCES. 


This faithful Committee, with tireless energy, presents a clear balance sheet. In 
the midst of continued calls for the Building Fund, it is something for which the 
Association should be specially thankful that the current expenses have been met 
and all the debts paid promptly. The members do not realize how much they are 
indebted to the Finance Committee. 

MEMBERSHIP. 


The Membership shows a decrease of 63, the total this year being 1070. This is due 
to the great decrease in the attractions which have been offered, and many are 
waiting until we enter the New Building before they renew their tickets. 


EXTENSION FUND. 


This is a newer department. Through it we seek to impress upon members the 
importance of systematic giving in aid of work for less favored young men at home and 
abroad. Special Bible Addresses are given on this topic at the regular meetings. It 
will be seen that over $400 has been received. This should be doubled next year and 
become an educational agency of primary importance in the work of the Association. 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


The admirable report of this department shows the efficiency and energy with which 
they have carried on their work, notwithstanding the many and serious disadvantages. 
The Directors feel that this department enables the Association at present (and will 


in the future, to a far greater extent), to reach and influence the sons of our 
subscribers and citizens, thus bringing the work into closer affiliation with the 
churches and homes of the City. 


THE WORKING FORCE. 


Apart from the Board of Directors, there has been 21 Sub-Committees, with a 
working membership of 144. With but few exceptions, these 21 Committees have 
held regular Monthly Meetings, where their work has been discussed and plans 
matured. The Boys Department has had seven working Committees with 44 work- 
ing members. These Committees have also held their Monthly Meetings. 

The large amount of detail work which this represents has been done voluntarily. 
Apart from the direct results secured, the personal development in systematic methods 
of Christian work is a most important factor. The main feature of the Association 
work is the development of its Acteve Members. Each member trained is so much 
added strength for the future. The Directors will be asked to consider how they can 
give this the attention it demands. 


RELIGIOUS WORK. 


Two hundred and ninety-eight (298) Religious Meetings have been held, with a 
total attendance of 14,187 young men. At these services hundreds of young men 
have sought and received counsel concerning entrance upon the Christian life. With 
increased facilities, the Directors will hope to hold from time to time series of Men’s 
Meetings, where greater prominence can be given to this agressive effort in bringing 
men to a decision for Christ. It is impossible to record the number of personal calls 
upon young men, which have been made by Secretaries and members, nor the number 
of those who have bzen won from darkness to light and from the power of Satan 
unto God. They have been not a few, many are now on our present staff of 
workers. Two Bible Classes and four Training Classes have been continued each 
week. I4 of our members, after receiving training, have undertaken work 
as Sunday School Teachers or Mission Workers. The weak point in the Religious 
work is in the difficulty of ‘‘ following up” promptly and satisfactorily hundreds of 
cases of personal interest, which comes in the line of daily work, as well as through 
the meetings. Some of the Associations now devote the time of one of the 
Secretaries wholly to this essential branch. This is the only possible solution of the 
question. The Directors will also be called upon to consider this question at an early 


date. 
BRANCHES, 


So soon as the work is begun in the Central Building on Dominion Square the 
question of City extension should be taken up. Building lots should be secured in 
Point St. Charles and the North East End and held for the Association. In order 
to fulfil its responsibility towards the young men of the city, this Association should 
have three branches, in addition to the Central Building, and all under one control. 

For summer work, Athletic grounds are a necessity now. Next year, with the 
Physical Department under full headway, this will be a greater necessity. 

The reports of the 21 Sub-Committees which are presented: to-night give some 
idea of the extent of the work for the past year and the results obtained. 


6 


The Directors desire to acknowledge the goodness of God in the trying experi- 
ences of the past year, and are specially grateful that they have been all of one mind 
and have sought to work with one aim in view, viz. the extension of God’s Kingdom 
amongst the young men of the City. 

On behalf of the J)irectors, 


D. A. BUDGE.

EXECUTIVE. 


The employees of the Association have been the same as the previous year and 
have given unqualified satisfaction, Mr. Orr dividing his time between the Associa- 
tion proper and developing the work at Point St. Charles, where services have been 
regularly held as a foundation for definite work, which we trust soon to be in a » 
position to undertake there. 

The Home and Foreign Extension Fund Committee has been regularly organized, 
and is proving its usefulness in the education of its members in systematic giving. 
This has enabled the Association to help very materially the development of our work 
in India. 

The Volunteer Camp work was successfully carried out under the ahielation and 
assistance of Mr. Patton. | 

Special sermons to young men were preached by most of the City Pastors on 
Sunday, Nov. 7th, and in this connection we have to record our obligation to the 
Ministers generally of our City, for their increased sympathy and practical help in 
our work. 

We are happy to announce the success of the Committee in securing the services 
of Mr. W. H. Ball as Physical Director. Mr. Ball is a graduate of the Spring- 


7 


field School, is specially qualified for the position, and commences his work with us 
first of September next. 

The Anniversary meeting was held on January 27th in the St. James Methodist 
Church, which was crowded to overflowing, and much interest manifested. We are 
gratified at this indication that our friends are in growing accord with our methods 
and look upon our anniversary occasions as specially attractive. 

The year has been somewhat broken, because of the time necessarily given to the 
details of the new Building, but we wish to acknowledge with gratitude the guiding 


hand of God and evidences of his favor and approval. 
R. H. HOLLAND, 


Chairman. 


NEW BUILDING. 


When your Committee last reported to you, about a year ago, they had hopes 
of being able about this time, or very soon after, to give you over the new building 
finished and ready for the great work for Christ and the souls of men, for which it 
is intended, and for which we hope it may be long used. This, you all know, 
has been rendered impossible by reason of the accident which happened to the 
building, or rather, to a small part of the interior of it, for as many of you are 
aware, the break-down only happened to a very small portion of it. The Gym- 
nasium, Halls, upper flats and much the larger part of the interior, as well as 
the whole outside walls and roof not having moved at all, but only having been 
proved to be exceptionally strong by reason of the severe strain and test to which 
they were thus so suddenly and unexpectedly exposed. 

Your Committee is having the building completed just as speedily as it can, 
and though the work sometimes seems to move slowly, yet it appears to them that 
the further they go on with the work the more they are satisfied with the style and 
plan of the building and the more it seems to be suited for the purpose for which it 
is being erected. 


FINANCES, 
Your Committee estimated some time ago, that the Building, when completed,

Since this estimate was made an elevator has been found absolutely necessary, 
for the working of the upper flats, adding another $2,000 to the cost of the building, 
so that we may say that in addition to the mortgage, $16,000 will be required 
to meet the Account as at present estimated. This amount your Committee would 
very much like to see all subscribed, and when this is done, which we hope will be 
very shortly, it would seem as if the Young Men’s Christian Association, in its New 
Building, had a clear and bright future before it. 


8 


The rents to be received are expected to cover all interest on the mortgage and 


leave a good moderate amount over, to be applied as the Association may think best. 


FURNISHING. 


Your Committee thought that the furnishing of the New Rooms might be done 


best by the various Churches in the City, and accordingly have called in the aid of 


the Ladies in these Churches. 


We may say, that from the very kind and cordial 


manner your Subscription Committee has been received by these ladies, we have little 
doubt, but that all that is required for the furnishing of all, except the Hall and 
Gymnasium, will be supplied from this source. Many of the friends of the Associa- 
tion might be able to help the matter on in their different churches.

DAVID YUILE, 


Chatrnian. 


FINANCE. 


At the beginning of the current year, as usual, the various committees made a care- 
ful estimate of the sums they expected to require for their work and, after these were 
duly considered by the Finance Committee, appropriations were made to each depart- 
ment. 

It is very gratifying to be able to say that each Committee has been able to keep 
its expenditure within its allowance. Owing to the monthly presentation of these 
accounts, it was necessary that provision should be made for monthly disbursement, 
thus requiring the Committee to go out collecting every month of the year. Though 
this may seem a very taxing undertaking and is indeed so, yet when met heartily by 
the friends, which has been so generally the case, the Committee have cheerfully 
given this labor, and now take this opportunity of gratefully alluding to the generous 
reception which has been so uniformly accorded them even in the face of drafts for 
the Building Fund. 

As in the past, the Committee are deeply indebted to Mr. A. G. Olive for his 
valuable services in keeping the accounts. 

WARDEN KING, 
Chairman.

ROOMS AND LIBRARY. 


Your Committee beg leave to report that on account of the proposed removal of 
the new library and the repairs necessary to the present one, this department of the 
work has not been prosecuted with the usual energy. However, 49 new books were 
purchased and a large number were replaced at a cost of $118.75 During the year 
there were over 5000 books drawn by 550 readers. The number of books now in the 
library is 3057. Since the close of the library, your Committee have been diligently 
selecting names of books to be added, and studying the latest system of numbering 
and cataloguing, preparatory to greatly extending the usefulness of the library in our 
new quarters. Your Committee regret the loss of a number of books and the un- 
necessary trouble given to the librarians by those who have held books beyond the 
time allowed... It is not right that our overworked officers should be compelled to 
write again and again or call at the residences of careless members for books overdue. 


STATEMENT. 
550 readers. 


5855 books drawn during the year. 

49 books added to library during year, and a large number replaced. 
$220 spent on supplying reading room. 

$118.75 spent on library. 


F. W. KELLY; 


Chatrnian.

We very much regret that we cannot make a better shewing at the close of this. 
year. 

Your Committee have earnestly endeavoured to keep up the membership to its. 
old standard, and if possible, increase it; but we have had to contend with many 
difficulties during the past season, which we trust will entirely disappear when we 
enter our new and splendidly equipped building. We would solicit the earnest co- 
operation of all our friends in this work, and we feel confident, with the bright future 
that lies before us, we may expect a very large increase during the coming season. 


A. R. WIGHTMAN, 


Chairman. 


EXTENSION WORK. 


Organized some two years ago this work is still new to the larger. portion of our 
members. It started in the form of a missionary band, by holding a few meetings and 
receiving subscriptions ; since then it has taken more definite lines, confining itself to 
the development of association work amongst young men, especially those of India 
and Japan, and aiding the International and Inter- Provincial Committees in supervising 
the work in the United States and Canada. The development of young men for 
secretaries has not been overlooked, and the Committee has devoted part of their funds 
to the above object. 

India has been specially chosen as the object of our support at the request of 
the International Committee, and the results show that the choice was a wise one. 
It is only three years ago that Mr. David McConaughy was appointed to the 
position of Secretary at Madras and to supervise the work in India. The holding 
of the first National Conference in January last shows a wonderful advancement 
in the work, there being present no less than 35 delegates from 17 Associations, 
besides representatives from four other towns, where as yet no associations exist, and 
resulted in appointing a National Committee to direct the India work. To this work, 
50 per cent. of the funds of the Committee are devoted. The remainder of the funds 
are divided as follows: 20 per cent. to the work of the Provincial Committee, 
20 per cent. to the training of young men as Secretaries, and 10 per cent. 
to the International Committee’s work. 

Since starting, the Committee has paid out for the support of these objects $825, 
but feel that much more should be done. No one is barred from subscribing, 
amounts being received from 2 to 50 cents per week. During the past year there have 
been 30 subscribers to this fund. We feel that the small number is owing to the 
many calls upon the members arising from the new building. 

The Committee are now conferring with the chairmen of all other committees, 
with the object of bringing this important work before each committee man personally, 
the junior department being included, and we trust this may result in greatly 
increasing the committee’s power to help on this work for young men. Each member 
should have a personal interest in their fellow young men, and one of the best and 
most direct ways of doing so is by subscribing to this fund. The field is a vast one, 
and no time should be lost in following up and furthering the advantages already 
gained.

RECEPTION COMMITTEE. 


The nine meetings which were held of this Committee had an average attendance 


of ten. 
389 men have been on duty during 286 nights, being an average of more than 


one man each night. 

The rooms were closed each evening with devotional exercises when practicable. 

The total number of evening visitors during the year was 13,546. Three were 
introduced to churches, eleven signed the pledge, and twenty-three were spoken to 
personally regarding their soul’s welfare. 

Besides the inside work, the members have called upon strangers in the city and 
brought them to the Association meetings. 

The Committee assisted at the New Year’s Reception, and also supplied ushers 
at the Anniversary, the W.C.T.U. and Evangelical Alliance meetings. 

Messrs. Stevenson and Paterson represented this Committee at the Convention 


in Kingston. 
G. F. PATERSON, 


Chairman, 


18 


SOCIAL COMMITTEE. 


Your Committee at this, the close of another Association year, begs to present its 
report of the social work carried on in connection with the Association, as follows :— 

At the beginning of the season, the idea of having a recognized evening in each 
week for social work, on which an informal programme might be presented, was, after 
consideration, decided against, owing chiefly to the building being occupied in other 
ways on most evenings, and the fact that the Secretaries had already more work on 
hand than they could conveniently carry on. 

Social meetings for members and friends were held during the months of October, 
November and February, which proved on the whole very satisfactory. The 
attendance was fair and in some cases sufficient to crowd the parlors, and it is 
hoped that they may have proved, not only entertaining, but of a lasting benefit to 
many who were present thereat. These meetings had unfortunately to be omitted 
during the months of March, April and May, owing to the uncertainty respecting 
the repairs to the present building. 

While the usual reception was not held on New Year’s Day, a select pro- 
gramme was arranged for the evening and was carried out with great success. The 
parlors were filled to overflowing, and the general impression seemed to be that it 
was one of the best entertainments held in the Association Building for some time. 

In concluding this Report, your Committee desires to express to the many friends 
who have aided it in accomplishing its work, and especially to the ladies of the 
churches, its hearty thanks for the valuable services rendered. 

G. A. IRWIN, 
Chairman. 


EMPLOYMENT. 


This bureau has not had an opportunity of shewing what might be done; the 
great pressure of work has prevented proper time and attention being given to this 
department. 

The gratitude of young men for any assistance rendered towards securing employ- 
ment amply repays any effort expended, though many are careless about reporting. 

We cannot but speak of a growing impression, which, if true, cannot but fail to be 
of serious injury to commercial life, as one brother puts it: ‘* There appears among 
young men a seeking after positions rather than a fitness for them.” 

What the country needs is men of character, who know one business. With 
pleasure we have assisted several of our members towards securing positions of trust 
and responsibility. We can recommend such men, as the Association has proved no 
mean training school in business methods.

ATHLETIC COMMITTEE. 


The work of this Committee has, during the past year, been pushed most -vigor- 
ously, and as a result the different clubs under our control are in as good, if nota 
better position than ever before. 

Lacrosse practice was started early in the summer of last year, on the Exhibition 
Grounds, which were kindly granted us for that purpose by the Grounds’ Committee, 
and continued 3 mornings each week from 6 to 7 o’clock throughout the summer, the 
average attendance being about 14. 

During the season two friendly matches were played with City Clubs ; the first was 
lost by 3 too; the second was won by 6 to 0, so that at present there is a balance of 3 
goals standing to our credit. 

A Football Club, to play under Association rules, was organized in the Fall, and 
though most of its members had to be introduced to the game, the end of the season 
shewed a record, out of seven games played, of 3 won, 3 lost and 1 drawn, with a 
grand total of 17 goals scored against 16 by our opponents. 

This Spring has shewn the interest in the Football Club to be growing, and great 
things are looked for during the year. 

The records of most of our City Clubs shew that for some time past Snow-Shoeing 
has been steadily on the decline as a popular sport, and unhappily our Club has 
failed to shew itself an exception in this respect. Although the winter was all that 
could be desired, it was very seldom the attendance at our tramps numbered more than 
a ‘*baker’s dozen.” 

Indoor athletics have also claimed some part of the attention of the Committee, 
and as a result of its efforts several men went in for a course of systematic training 
during the winter at one or other of the large City Gymnasia, for the express purpose 
of being in a position to lend the instructor a helping hand in his work at the new 


20) 


Gymnasium, and too much credit can hardly be given to these men for so speedily 
shewing this practical interest in our new work. 

In closing, the Committee most earnestly recommend that more of the active 
members of the Association take an interest in the athletic work and make it what it 
really is, viz., one means to the great end. Opportunities for personal work are here 
in plenty, for nowhere will a pleasant, cheery nod or smile be appreciated, a good 
example followed, or an earnest word taken to heart more readily than on the field 
or in the gymnasium. 

The fee to the athletic department is $1.00 per annum, which includes admission 
to all matches as well as practice games. Let every one here present determine to 
give the Committee their support during the year just opened, and may each and every 
one of us realize as Paul realized, that whether we eat or drink, or whatsoever we 
do, it should be all done to the glory of God. 

| J. DOIG, 


Chairman. 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


The Committees have performed their allotted work, and those who have acted 
on them have received practical training in this branch of the work which will show 
itself.forth in future years of the Association. 

We have noticed a marked development in christian work and service in the 
christian boys and workers, and we also feel that the department as a whole is in 
better working than ever before. 

Having felt a great need of definitely following up inquirers and young converts, 
a training class for building them up by Bible study has been held and found to be 
an invaluable aid in this direction. Two courses of study have been taken up. A 
difficulty met with has been in imparting to the boys the responsibility of working 
for Christ ; but we believe this has been remedied by our training classes, in which this 
matter has been fully brought forward. We feel that this is the most valuable agent 
in our work, which those who have been attending them do. Three classes have been 
regularly held and well attended. 

A need of having a building where the boys’ work can be carried on entirely — 
by itself, and thereby giving greater opportunities of reaching and holding them, has 
been more and more felt this year, and it is with feelings of joy that we look forward 
to the New Building, where this plan is proposed. 

We also feel the need of a Secretary who will be able to devote his whole time to 
this department. 

At the request of this Department, a recommendation was sent to the Provincial 
Committee, to have ‘‘ boys’ work” brought prominently before the Kingston Con- 
vention. ‘This was agreed, and a paper was presented by Mr. Percy H. Cushing. — As 
a result, a new interest was awakened for work among boys, which led to the revival of 
old meetings and the formation of new. 

““ Systematic giving” has been prominently tal our meetings, with a very fair 
result, some of our members becoming contributors to the extension fund.

Friday evening meeting has been held during the year without intermission.

SOCIAL WORK. 


Two members have been on duty Friday evenings, to welcome, entertain and 
introduce strangers. 

A social was held 24th November, 1890, at the opening of the winter work, 250 
being present, who thoroughly enjoyed the entertainment provided. 


ATHLETIC WORK. 


During the year 2 outings and 2 paper chases were held. 

This was the banner year for the S. S. Club. Organized 28th November with a 
membership of 75. It held tramps on Saturday afternoons to Athletic Club House and 
closed its season with a drive to same place. This was open to members of the 
department and participated in by about 150. 


MONETARY WORK. 


Deposits in Bank at end of year $1,243.24, an increase over previous year of 
$263.12 

Mr. Hague kindly gave 10 per cent. interest on the year’s savings, which amount, 
added to 4 per cent. from Canadian Bank of Commerce, made a very nice income. 


INVITATION WORK. 


This work has been carried on by personal work ; through the medium of the 
schools, by card and black-board notices ; and in S. S. Schools through Teachers and 
Superintendents. 


BRANCH WORK. 


The Meetings at Cote St. Antoine have been held in a room kindly furnished by 
the Methodist Institute, where a fortnightly Meeting has been conducted. A Com- 
mittee has been formed to supervise the work, with Mr. W. E. Cushing as Chairman. 
They are doing good work. 

In closing this report, we would say that we feel that the work of the year will, 
under God’s Holy Spirit, who alone can give the increase, be felt in the future of the 
Association of this City to the glory of God. 

R. L. CHARLTON, 


Chairman. 


22 
LITERARY SOCIETY. 


The average attendance has been 21, an increase of 3 upon last year. 

At date of making this report, there are 39 members on roll, an increase of 5. 

The following Officers were elected October 23rd :—Mr. H. B. Ames, President ; 
Mr. H. Bragg, Ist Vice-President; Mr. J. Allardice, 2nd Vice-President ; Mr. F. 
Taylor, Secretary. 

Debates were held and papers discussed as follows :— 

October 9th.—Debate, ‘‘ That a country-bred boy is more likely to succeed in business 
than one bred in the city.” 

October 23rd.—Election of Officers—Paper by H. B. Ames, ‘‘Is the condition of 
the working class improving ?” 

November 13.—Debate, ‘‘ That combines controlling the production of special com- 
modities are advantageous to a nation.” 

November 28th.—Reading by G. A. Dunlop, ‘‘ Vanity and Vanities;” paper by 
H. Bragg, ‘‘ Co-operation and Profit Sharing.” 

December 11th.—Debate, “ That Montreal needs a more thorough enforcement of 
the Temperance Laws that exist, rather than additional legislation. ” 

January 8th.—Reading by F. Taylor, ‘‘The Military Young Gentleman ;”’ paper by 
W. T. Castle, ‘‘ Confederation.” 

January 22nd.—Debate “That the Rebellion of 1837 was justifiable.” 

February 12.—Paper by W. T. Leach, ‘‘An evening with Dickens.” 

February 26.—Paper by H. B. Ames, ‘‘ Independence in Canadian Politics ;” read- 
ing by W. J. Orr, Extracts from Congressman Morse’s Speech in Washington 
on ‘Good Men in Politics.” 

March 12.—Debate, ‘‘ That poverty is more productive of crime than luxury.” 

March 26.—Reading by H. Bragg, ‘‘ Beson Ben:;” paper by J. Allardice, 
** Socialism. ” 

Nearly all who attended our meetings regularly were willing when called upon to 
take part in debates, and find that they have been greatly benefited from the study 
which such an undertaking involves, besides the practice they have had in public 
speaking. 


H. B. AMES, 
President. 


YOUNG MEN’S MEETING. 


The interest in, and attendance at, our Saturday night meeting still go on increasing 
year by year. Many young men have been brought to Christ during the past year— 
directly through this service. Scarcely a night has passed when there were no 
enquirers. These have been conversed with by workers, the acceptance of Christ 
pressed upon them, and their names sent to the pastors of the different churches. The 
training classes have been a great help to the Committee, both in training them and 
furnishing new workers. During the past year, the Committee have tried to each 
choose a man in the meeting—pray for him and speak to him after the meeting. 
This method has borne good results. 


23 


This meeting gives an opportunity for personal work. We heartily invite all our 
members, who would like to win souls for the Master, to come and help in this most 
promising field. Many who are now working with us date their conversion to a 
certain Saturday night. 

The musical department has been faithfully conducted by Mr. Wildman. Most 
of our good singers and players are at choir practice Saturday night, which renders it 
difficult to secure as large an orchestra and choir as we would like. 

The many pleasant memories that linger in our hearts in connection with the old 
building make us sad at the thought of leaving. We close this year with the prayer, 
‘“‘ If thy presence go not with us, carry us not up hence.” 


JOHN DUMARESQ, 
Chairman. 


SUNDAY MORNING BIBLE CLASS. 


Early last spring, our leader Mr. Patton resigned to enter the Springfield School 
for training secretaries, and at the request of the Committee Mr. S. S. Bain, although 
pressed with other duties, accepted the position, He has taught the class for eight 
months, and the members have been wonderfully blessed, as he has opened to us the 
Scriptures. Our lessons have been on the ‘‘ Life of our Lord,” as foretold in the Old 
and revealed in the New Testament, and also the “ Character of Joseph,” both of 
which have been very helpful, as the following testimonies will show :—One says, ‘‘I 
would rather go without my breakfast than miss one of these lessons ;” another, ‘‘ the 
lessons on the ‘‘ Life of our Lord”’ have been just what I wanted and have filled what 
was lacking in my life ;” still another, ‘‘ I see things in a new light.” It is with regret 
that we have been compelled to discontinue our class until Sept. Ist, owing to the 
alterations in this building. 

A regular system of visitation of the absentees was started at the beginning of the 
year and has been continued with success, the number visited being on an average 
15 monthly. 


Our average attendance at the class has been 23. 
ALEC ARTHUR. 


Chatrman. 


SUNDAY AFTERNOON EVANGELISTIC BIBLE CLASS. 


This Committee regret to have to report a falling off in the average attendance 
compared with that of the previous year, the figures being 90 and 73 respectively, and 
think that the unavoidable decrease in the number of Association privileges may 
account for this, in a measure at least. The highest figure reached was I19 on August 
24th, and the lowest was 51 on January 4th. 

The card system for the registration of the attendance has been used throughout 
the year, continuing to give the utmost satisfaction and proving itelf to be a source 
of much valuable statistical information. 386 letters and notices were sent to 
absentees, resulting in numbers of young men becoming constant in their attendance 
and eliciting many written replies acknowledging the class to have been a great 


24 


personal blessing, which help to recompense our Attendance Secretary and to encourage 
him in his special department. | 

From the beginning of our year until August, we continued our studies in the ever 
interesting Parables of Christ. | During September we considered special topics, and 
from October to the present time have been drawing lessons from Jewish history, run- 
ning from the ‘‘ Calling of Samuel” to the * Captivity in Babylon.” 

Two special addresses on Personal Purity were given, one in July by Mr. D. W. 
Ross and the other in November by Mr. J. R. Mott, College Secretary of the Inter- 
national Committee. These Services are of special value and were greatly blessed. 
On March 22nd, our old friends, Messrs. Corbett and Patton, with Mr. W. H. Davis, of 
the Springfield School, spoke on ‘‘ The Race of Life.” Together with the above 
named gentlemen, the thanks of the Committee are due to our friends in need, Mr. 
C. T. Williams, and to Mr. G. H. Craik, of the McGill College Association, for 
their kindness in conducting the class in Mr. Budge’s absence. 

This class is a free channel of much blessing, there seldom being a Sunday without 
some soul being awakened and brought to the Light. This year has also sent out its 
contingent of workers; seven of our members, Messrs. W. Y. Reid, T. O’Brien, H. Ky 
Ransom, Geo. Sleep, John Wilcock, Alex. Arthur and W. J. Orr having left us to 
become pioneers in the work at the Railway Branch at Point St. Charles, and at least 
a similar number have undertaken Sabbath School Work. Since January alone, seven 
members have gone to other cities. These figures, which, of necessity, are incom- 
plete, when considered with the transitory nature of our class, generally show that we 
are at a point of distribution which demands faithfulness in us in using our opportu- 
nities. 

The visitation of our sick was carefully attended to, bringing blessing both upon 
the sick and their visitors. We miss from amongst us Mr. Frank Teasdale, but 
recently called to his eternal rest in Christ Jesus. 

The Committee was represented at the Inter-Provincial Convention in February 
last by its Attendance Secretary, Mr. Charles Stevenson. 

The Committee is also greatly indebted to our organist, Mr. W. T. Walmsley, for 
his constant service, and to Mr. W. A. Coates, who has continued the monthly drill in 
new hymns throughout the year, thus greatly assisting the song service. { 

At this time this report would be incomplete were no mention to be made of the 
extraordinary strain borne by our beloved teacher, Mr. Budge, during the past year, 
and we rejoice for his sake that the time is coming soon, when, with the present 
anxious problems settled, he shall be at liberty to give his undivided attention to the 
work in one building. 

W. J. WRIGHT, 
Chairman, 


25 
TRACT DISTRIBUTION AMONG THE SAILORS. 


The distribution of tracts and papers among the sailors on the different vessels in 
the harbor commenced Sunday, May 4th, and continued throughout the summer until 
the end of November. The distributors met each Sunday in the Sailors’ Institute 
at 7.45 a.m., and after a brief season of prayer, started out to do their Master’s work. 

Our field of labor is the same as in previous years, from Windmill Point to 
Hochelaga, which is divided into sections, two or more workers having charge 
of each section. The attendance throughout has been very good. 

We cannot say what the results from this service are, but we know that it affords 
a grand opportunity for sowing the seed, and the results we leave with God. 


WILLIAM LAW, 
Chairnian. 


POINT ST. CHARLES. 


Work amongst the railroad men and young men of the ‘‘ Point” was commenced 
on a small scale early last year. A Training Class, under the leadership of Mr. 
W.J.Orr, which has met, on Friday evenings, at the different homes of the members, 
has had eight regular members on the roll, and an average attendance of four during 
the year. We feel that much benefit has been received by the Class. We have been 
instructed along the line of Christian work, more especially that of the work of the 
Young Men’s Christian Association, and believe we are much better fitted for service 
thereby. 

Through the kindness of the Grand Trunk Railway and the Committee of the G.T.R. 
Literary and Scientific Institute, we were granted the use of their Audience Hall for 
a Men’s Meeting on Sunday afternoons. This service was started on December 13th, 
1890, and has since been held without interruption each Sunday at 4.15. Total 
attendance for.above period 903, an average of 45 each day, nearly all of whom were 
railway men. The meetings which have been addressed by friends of the work, 
were interesting throughout and, we trust, profitable. The thanks of the Committee 
are tendered to these friends for their valuable assistance ; also to Mr. J. Wilcock, 
who has kindly officiated at the organ, and thereby rendered very acceptable service. 

Mr. W. K. Snider, Conductor G.T.R., Palmerston, Ont., visited us, and gave 
an address on Sunday afternoon, August 2nd, in the Grand Trunk Reading Rooms, 
to a large number of railroad men and friends. He also conducted meetings in 
connection with the Association in St. Matthew’s (Presbyterian) and Point St. Charles 
Methodist Churches several evenings following. Although the weather was exceed- 
ingly hot and stormy, attendance at these services was good. Several requests for 


prayer were made. ; 
THOS. O’BRIEN, 
Chairman. 


26 


INVITATION COMMITTEE. 


The attendance of this Committee has been very good during the past year. We 
have been greatly encouraged in our work, many young men having responded to the 
invitations given ; and we have faith to believe that the good seed sown in the meet- 
ings will spring up and bear fruit to the glory of God. We have not looked for 
results, but still they have come to us. One case is that of a young Englishman. 
Having just arrived in the city, a stranger, he was passing the Association one 
Saturday evening, when he was handed an invitation card, with a personal invitation 
to attend the meeting. He did so, and it was the means of his accepting Christ, and 
since he has been a worker on this Committee, until circumstances prevented his 
continuing. Invited first, then inviting. 

Many having taken up this work as young converts, are now actively engaged in 
church and mission work. One instance is that of Mr. H. Butteress, who, having 
returned to England, is now engaged in the Lord’s work there, having taken a class 
in the Sunday school, organized a Bible training class and a cottage prayer meeting. 

This Committee was represented by its Chairman at the Kingston Convention. 
What impressed him the most while there regarding our work was the paper on 
‘¢ Definite Personal Work.” Our Saturday night meeting is a good field for this. 
We desire not to lose the opportunities given, but, taking encouragement from the 
past, in the future ‘‘ Be not weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap, if we 


faint not.” 


E, J. WILLIAMS, 


Chairman.

CURRENT EXPENSES. 
———____—_/2,-—____— 


The Merchants and Citizens have in past years granted 
their liberal support to this work on behalf of the Young Men 
of the City. Proposed enlargement will require an increased 
financial constituency. The Committee therefore solicit the 
continued sympathy and co-operation of the citizens. 

Branches in connection with the Central Building should 
be opened in Point St. Charles and the North-East End. The 
Board of Directors hope to receive such support as will enable © 


them to carry out this very desirable work.
